div.p: This paper deals with the overload caused by excessive service requests from the environment for dynamic control systems. A method of providing gracefully degraded solutions is proposed, based on the previous work on the project dealing with the design for consistent embedded real-time control system with the goal of increasing its dependability. A syntax is defined as an enhancement of the object oriented extension of a standard real-time programming language. Further, the task program execution times are estimated for possible execution paths, providing the necessary basis for schedulability analysis in both normal and critical operation modes.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Computer control systems are increasingly involved in our everyday life. They can be frequently found in safety critical applications where integrity of the system substantially depends on them. Their failure could have severe consequences: it may result in massive material loss or endanger human safety.

Several adequate paradigms and methods for the design of embedded control systems already exist but the ones most commonly used are usually unsatisfactory. In general, designers either use widely available and well known tools from universal computing, or none, and program their off-the-shelf microprocessor based hardware platforms by implementation languages like C or C++, or assembly language. Such designs very often also use non-adequate scheduling policies, usually the fixed priority based ones as implemented in microprocessors.

In consist,ently designed dynamic systems, which need t o deal with sporadic events, the most commonly accepted and feasible scheduling policies are deadline driven, most notable being earliest deadline first strategy. So that all their deadlines are met, a new schedule is calculated from the read? tasks' parameters on arrival of each new request. However, provision should be made for the case of dynamic overload: when the system is incapable of serving all of them, which should not actually happen in properly designed applications.

In this paper we do not intend to provide revolutionary solutions to the problem. It is obvious that in such cases the load must be reduced in order to allow the system to survive. Hence, the performance must be degraded gracefully by switching from full implementation to a subset of minimal functions.

The main contribution of this partial project is to introduce language means and operating system support to e-mail: colnaricldomen.verber@uni-mb.si perform this in a consistent and controlled way. It also allows for consideration of such reduced tasks' execution times in the alternative task set run-time schedulability analysis. In this paper, an intermediate report on our ongoing work is given. This paper is organised as follows: in Sections 2 and 3 some background will be presented in order t o explain some of the solutions from our previous research which then provide the necessary basis for this proposed implementation. The outline of an object oriented real-time programming language will be presented, which has been devised by our group. In Section 4 possible causes, classification and possibilities for prevention of overload situations will be elaborated. The implementation will be proposed in Section 5 where consideration will also be given to its effect on tasks' execution time estimation.

div.head: BACKGROUND: TASKING A N D OPERATING SYSTEM DESIGN OUTLINES
div.p: In this and the next section some solutions from the background projects are given which are relevant to the proposed dealings with overload situations.

For the last ten years, we have been developing hardware platforms which are all based on an asymmetrical multiprocessor architecture consisting of two types of processors: task processors, on which application tasks are being processed, and dedicated OS kernel processor, allowing for parallel execution of OS routines. Similar implementation can be found in other projects [l]: ['2]. At this moment we consider all application tasks t o be statically mapped onto the task processors because of the hardwired peripheral interfaces, so no migration between them is possible. For details please refer to [ 3 ] , [4], [5].
This architecture has two advantages:

. events from the environment are normally introduced to the system by interrupts. Their handling obviously delays execution of the tasks, if they are run on the same processor, and thus prevents temporal determinism and run-time estimation. In our case, events are handled in parallel with the task execution; the latter is only preempted if it is absolutely necessary in order t o provide for all tasks to meet their deadlines, and under consistent supervision of the operating system.

. parallel execution of system routines on a separate processor guarantees better system performance since the task processor is almost exclusively dedicated t o task program execution. Furthermore, it allows more complex OS service for the same reason.

The latter advantage is also exploited in overload hanthe increased dling implementation as proposed below: complexity of OS services does not further delay task execution since it is done on a separat,e processor.

Communication between the task and the kernel processor is done via a few locations of a dual-port RAM accessible from both sides. This is feasible since the system is not supposed to be geographically distributed, and the number of task processors is limited (for the time being we are considering three task processors). Task and kernel processors are synchronised using polling and, if necessary: hardware signals.

The earliest deadline first (EDF) scheduling policy was adopted, being optimal for the proposed architecture. Conceptually, it already introduces run-time schedulabilit! analysis which upon the occurrence of a task detects whether it will eventually cause overload, and thus initiates handling before this occurs. We refer to [4] for details of the modified EDF scheduling and schedulability analysis used in our model.

Scheduling and run-time schedulability analysis are done on the kernel processor. thus introducing no delay. It, was possible, for this reason! t o add some additional functions which handle the oi.erload sit,uations without increasing the run time overhead.

div.p: The object orieiited programming language Object-PE-iRL has been devised [6] A similar approach as in C++ was used for introduction of classes: a class is defined as an extension to the s t r u c t u r e . It was decided not t o iniplement multiple inheritance because of simplicity of code generation and esecution time analy-sis. All traditional elements of classes were included (i.e. variables, methods, constructors and destructors). Like other object,-oriented languages. Ob-jectPEARL also supports polymorphism through virtual methods. How this can be employed t o deal with overload situations, it will be shown later in the paper.

In addition, special types of variables were introduced called virtual variables or properties. Properties behave as ordinary variables with two associated methods. The first method is used for reading the variable and the second is used to change its value. Properties operate in a similar manner as those used in the COM automation model [9]. There are also special kinds of properties which are declared only for specification purposes and no code is associated with them. They can represent certain non program-specific attributes.

In ObjectPEARL a task is considered as an object with a method which represents the main task behaviour and with several methods for tasking operations. A similar approach is used in Java [lo]. General task is thus declared as shown \ in Fig. 1. To further exploit the advantages of the object,-oriented approach. other traditional elements of real-time systems are also represented as classes and objects. To provide for this. a way was elaborated t o represent tasks, semaphores: bolts; signals etc. For example, a semaphore is declared as shoxn in Figure 2. As in tasks, private variables FCount and FSemaState are used for internal semaphore implementation. Again, private variables and implementation of methods are under direct control of the operating system. There is an additional parameter associated with the Request method that serves as deadline on waiting for the semaphore t o be released because of the need for temporal predictability of the programs in ObjectPEARL.

Benefits of the object oriented description can be fully utilised when there is already a wide set of predefined data types (classes) and when components are divided into specialised groups (e.g. periodic and a-periodic tasks).

div.head: Compiler for ObjectPEARL with integrated execution time analyser.
div.p: A compiler was implemented for the proposed language. The aim was to develop a modular and flexible compiler that could be easily modified based on results of theoretical research of the development environment. The compiler should also be independent on target-system although in its current version it only generates code for a single processor. Nevertheless, the compiler should generate efficient code, t.herefore several optimisation techniques were included into the compiler.

One of the most important features of the compiler/analyser was realistic estimation of worst-case task execution times (WCET), which is the basis for timing analysis at the higher levels [ll], [12], [13]. Support for automated direct measurement of program run time on the target hardware platform using Background Debugging Mode (BDM) facility of the selected microprocessor was developed to allow for as realistic estimations as possible.

Worst-case execution time analysis is performed in tn-o phases. In the first phase, structure of the program by means of blocks; loops, decisions, etc.: is identified. Then, the maximal execution times are estimated or measured for all linear parts of the code. High-level temporal analysis is then performed on the structure of the program using simple recursive rules [14].

In spite of all efforts, there is always a certain level of pessimism in run-rime estimation due to unknown runtime program behaviour. This includes the number of iterations of loops, or different alternatives in case and if statements, etc, when the longest alternative has always to be considered. During the progress of the task program: however, the remaining time can gradually become better estimated, since there are less and less unknown features involved. Therefore, i t is reasonable to update the residual execution time of the task during its execution.

The update clause was introduced for this reason, : it provides fresh update of estimated residual execution time of the task which overrides the run-time information in the task control block of the kernel processor. update can be automatically inserted into the task body by the compiler as soon as a significant improvement in the run time estimation can be anticipated (i.e. after the loops with very variable numbers of iterations, case and i f statements with alternative parts of very different lengths, procedures with variable execution time, etc.) In addition, the update time is automatically generated by the run time analyser.

Caution is necessary by excessive use of the update sentence, since it also introduces certain system overhead. It is reasonable to consider the tradeoff between the improved execution time estimation and the delay in execution of the task.

Because update generates the absolute value of the residual execution time, it can only be inserted within the task body and not in generic procedures or functions. It will be shown later in the paper how the concept of the update clause can be extended to deal with the overload situation.

Compiler for ObjectPEARL has been implemented us- ing Delphi development environment and runs on a %-indows 9x or Windows NT platform. It uses simple recursive descent parsing algorithm with semantic routines for code generation and temporal analysis. In its current version. it generates code for Motorola's ColdFire microcontroller.

Translation of ObjectPE.4RL code into the standard PEARL was also studied but there mere several semaiitic discrepancies between both languages (e.g. visibility of the class members). These differences could not be easily considered when using simple translation techniques.

div.head: Possible causes of overload situations.
div.p: Theoretically, it should always be possible to prevent overload situation by a proper a-priori schedulability analysis [13] which should be done at the design time. Unfortunately, in real life this is not always true for several reasons: i= 1 a system may issue service requests invoking tasks more frequently than specified. This is even more probable when the system is a t the edge of a stable operation or slightly beyond: all systems are reporting abnormal states thus flooding the control system with requests when its integrity is most needed; due to hardware or software failures in the system it may not behave according to the specifications which .

A n may cause the tasks to be executed improperly and their actual execution times are delayed; because of their complexity, there can always be errors in run-time estimation or schedulability analysis; a-priori schedulability analysis could yield pessimistic results and is thus impractical and unpopular with application designers (the implied pessimism calls for more expensive hardware platforms); for this reason the results of a-priori schedulability analysis are sometimes manually overridden in order to achieve better utilisation, risking transient overload in (possibly rare) cases which cannot easily be predicted. overload situation can be either transitive or permanent.

The main cause of the former is slightly higher frequency of asynchronous service requests violating the specifications temporarily. Measures to prevent actual deadline violation in such cases, which usually degrade the performance, are only employed once and can easily be tolerated. However, it has to be detected, reported and dealt with during the maintenance phase. Reasons for the permanent overload are usually either more serious errors in system specifications or run-time estimation, or hardware or software failures. Some overload situations can be prevented. E.g., frequency of the service requests can be monitored by a simple hardware watchdog timer: set to the minimal specified time and triggered upon occurrence of a request, it must always run out before the next one appears. In the case of an override, the request can be delayed if possible, or ignored, or an alert is reported so that the violation of the specifications can be detected before the system is jammed.

div.head: v. DEALING WITH OVERLOAD
div.p: Once an overload situation is detected it can only be handled with the same resources if the complexity of task processing is reduced. The application programmer must for that reason already in the early stages of the design consider minimal performance of the tasks, i.e. how the full functions of the system can be gracefully degraded in order to survive the overload situation.
It is not the intention of this paper to go into details of graceful degradation methods, but to present some ideas as t o how it can be implemented.

Overload situation occurred because it was impossible to meet the deadline of at least one task T k that is in the ready state, i.e. the residual execution time of the executing task plus the sum of all tasks to be scheduled before Tk (with closer deadlines) is longer than the time to its deadline. It is thus necessary to reduce the complexity of these tasks to allow T k to meet its deadline.
We are referring to that situation as the critical mode. In this mode, there are two groups of tasks that must be handled:
tasks that have already started execution (the actually running task and all those which have already been executing but were preempted.) tasks that have not been scheduled t,o run yet.

To handle the latter, tasks may have two bodies: a regular one which is fully implementing the task's requirements, and the alt,ernative one which onll-does the most essential functions with gracefully degraded performance. and which may possibly even be empty. Operating system is supplied with execution times of the task in both normal and critical mode.

It is obvious that the complete state of the task cannot be maintained in the critical mode. but only the subset which is required in order to keep the system's minimal integrity. The other system variables are kept in a stable and inactive position.

Tasks that were previously scheduled to run in a normal mode have already entered their regular body. If a situation later becomes critical they cannot rewind to the start and enter the alternative body but must reduce their complexity if feasible and terminate as soon as possible.

To allow for this it is here proposed to implement procedures (in form of class methods) in the same two ways again: the normal and the critical alternati1.e. This can be implemented with virtual methods in a similar n a y as polymorphism: depending on the mode reported by the kernel processor from the I'irtual hfethod Table (I*7AIT) the according address of the method is retrieved and the method executed.

In a similar way to the tasks that are entirely run in t,he critical mode, it is also impossible for the ones that, had to be switched into it during their execution to niaintain the complete state of the task once in a critical mode, but only its necessary subset. The other stat,es. which are not absolutely necessary for the minimal integrity of t,he sJ-stem and which may have been already prei-iously activated: must be disabled before the continuation of the task in the critical mode. If this is impossible: the task must be run to its termination in the full performance mode.

Such consideration is required in the case when in certaiii procedure peripheral interfaces, common variables and/or synchronisers have already been modified but their handling was not finished. In these cases it has to be decided whether switching into the critical mode, and thus interruption of the procedure, is reasonable and safe. For t.he time being the decision on that is considered responsibility of the application designer.

It is possible, especially in the case of temporal ox-erload, that by executing tasks in the critical mode, the latter ceases to exist. To check for this, rescheduling can he attempted; since it is done in parallel on the operating system kernel processor it does not require any additional resources. Three cases must be considered:
For the tasks that have not been running yet their normal execution times will be considered, and these tasks will eventually be run in normal mode.

It is different for the tasks that have already executed in the critical mode. It may be decided by the application designer that switching back t o normal mode could be done, i.e. the system state is such that after a checkpoint continuation in both critical or normal mode is possible. 0 If this does not hold, the task has to be run in critical state until its termination. This generally happens if some states necessary for the continuation in the normal mode were not properly maintained during the task's operation in the critical mode. Decision is again left to the application designer.

The proposed syntax is given in Figure 3. Alternative procedures must have the same name, same set of parameters and both must be declared as virtual. Because the parameters and optional result type must be the same: their re-declaration in the alternative procedure is unnecessary.

div.p: The designer is. through the syntax, encouraged to consider the design of alternative task bodies and methods from the early stages in the design. He or she is also always aLvare through the automated execution time analysis what time saving heishe achieved by certain implementation and can decide n-hether further degradation of performance is necessary.

Let us consider the following case as an example: The procedure Newton normally calculates the root of a function. By the analysis of the function it has been shown that, at most. 20 iterations of the loop will be necessary to reach the desired precision of 0.001. In the critical mode, however: a less accurate result with the precision of 0.1 is acceptable, which may have been already obtained in 3 iterations, thus requiring only one fourth of the calculation time. Methods which are called in the alternative bodies of tasks or alternative implementations of methods is obviously the shortest possible. For this reason, once in the critical mode, the critical alternative procedure is always automatically invoked if it exists.

A checkpoint consists of a modified update statement: to minimise the communication overhead only the index of its entry in the table in TCB is reported to the OS kernel processor. Furthermore, with update the running task polls whether the system is in the normal or critical situation.

In the example in Figure 7 it is shown how the update statement can improve the run time estimation: the task controls the speed of a motor by acquiring its current value and accelerating or braking it. Normally, the motor will run at the normal speed and no action is necessary; the latter is only required when increasing or decreasing the load.

In addition, in the case of critical mode, acceleration or braking could be done more roughly with less demanding algorithms: although the motor control was active. it was done faster than considered in normal task execution time estimation. Again, the actual residual t,inie should be updat,ed. Once an overload situation is detected during the normal scheduling procedure. the operating system enters the critical mode. This is made available to the running task in the task processor by setting a flag ( c r i t ) .

The set of tasks which are in ready states is now rescheduled with alternative execution times. The given critical times are taken for all tasks that were not executing yet. The residual execution times are calculated for the executing task and for those which wait for re-scheduling after they have been preempted: the saving in time gained by switching into the critical mode from the next checkpoint on, is subtracted from their normal residual time. This saving is calculated at the compile time and is available in the TCB table at the entry belonging to the last checkpoint the task has encountered.

The running task becomes aware of the critical situation when it first executes an update statement and polls the crit flag. The alternative implementations of the methods will be executed from now on.

The main structure of the task, however, is unchanged. If this is not desired (e.g. the algorithm performed is long, but unnecessary in the case of critical mode), a part of the task body can simply be put in a method where alternative solutions are possible.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION
div.p: The approach proposed in this paper deals with temporary overload situations that may occur for various reasons during the execution of processes. In such situations the load must be reduced by degrading the performance; after the critical situation is cleared the system may return to the normal mode.

Inclusion of overload handling into the syntax has another advantage, namely to encourage the programmer to already have considered possible overload situations during the design of the regular task program, as opposed t o the usual practice of attempting to solve the problem postfest,um. Robustness of the system is increased by providing less demanding alternative solutions, as a side effect.
-4s a last resort in overload handling, an alternative at the highest level (i.e. of the main task) should provide for fail safe behaviour: shutting down the system into a safe state.

In this proposed solution, the system is programmed t o behave in two alternative ways. The challenge for future work is to provide for gradual graceful degradation: to provide more than two solutions and to find the right level of degradation according to the tightness of the schedule. Although this would seem to use a lot of overhead on the operating system side, it is feasible because it is processed on the operating system kernel processor in parallel with the task execution, and, therefore, does not take its resources.
